flawed_step: The natural proof tries to rebuild G from L(G): each vertex v of G is matched to the clique in L(G) formed by the edges at v, and then G's vertices are read off from those cliques. This step fails. A triangle in L(G) can come from three edges sharing one vertex (a star K_{1,3}) or from the three edges of a triangle K3. L(G) alone cannot tell these apart, so G cannot always be recovered. Whitney's theorem only works once the pair K3 / K_{1,3} is excluded.
counterexample: G1 = K3 (triangle) and G2 = K_{1,3} (star with 3 leaves). Both are connected and simple. In each graph every two of the 3 edges share an endpoint, so L(G1) ≅ L(G2) ≅ K3. But G1 has 3 vertices and G2 has 4, so they are not isomorphic.
assessment_summary: The statement is false. The key step of the proof, rebuilding G from the cliques of L(G), breaks down because a triangle in L(G) may come from either a star or a triangle in G. K3 and K_{1,3} are both connected and both have line graph K3, yet they are not isomorphic. Whitney's line-graph isomorphism theorem does hold for connected graphs, but only when this one pair is excluded.
